facts.statement: The type species of the genus Stegoceras is Stegoceras validum.
facts.quote: type_species: Stegoceras validum

facts.statement: Stegoceras lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 77.5 to 74 million years ago.
facts.quote: Stegoceras is a genus of pachycephalosaurid (dome-headed) dinosaur that lived in what is now North America during the Late Cretaceous period, about 77.5 to 74 million years ago (mya).

facts.statement: The first specimens of Stegoceras were found in Alberta, Canada, and described in 1902.
facts.quote: The first specimens from Alberta, Canada, were described in 1902, and the type species Stegoceras validum was based on these remains.

facts.statement: Stegoceras was a small, bipedal dinosaur measuring 2 to 2.5 meters in length and weighing between 10 and 40 kilograms.
facts.quote: Stegoceras was a small, bipedal dinosaur about 2 to 2.5 m long, and weighed around 10 to 40 kg.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the skull of Stegoceras was flat in juveniles and developed a dome shape as the animal aged.
facts.quote: The skull is thought to have been flat in juvenile animals and to have grown into a dome with age.

facts.statement: Stegoceras was likely herbivorous and probably possessed a good sense of smell.
facts.quote: Stegoceras was most likely herbivorous, and it probably had a good sense of smell.

facts.statement: The function of the skull dome in Stegoceras is debated, with theories including combat, sexual display, or species recognition.
facts.quote: The function of the dome has been debated, and competing theories include use in intra-specific combat (head or flank-butting), sexual display, or species recognition.

facts.statement: The first remains of Stegoceras were collected by Lawrence Lambe from the Belly River Group in Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: The first known remains of Stegoceras were collected by palaeontologist Lawrence Lambe from the Belly River Group, in the Red Deer River district of Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: Initial specimens included partial skull domes collected in 1898 and 1901, now housed in the Canadian Museum of Nature.
facts.quote: These remains consisted of two partial skull domes (specimens CMN 515 and CMN 1423 in the Canadian Museum of Nature) from two animals of different sizes collected in 1898, and a third partial dome (CMN 1594) collected in 1901.

facts.statement: Lawrence Lambe described and named the genus Stegoceras and the species Stegoceras validus in 1902 based on these specimens.
facts.quote: Based on these specimens, Lambe described and named the new monotypic genus and species Stegoceras validus in 1902.

facts.statement: John Bell Hatcher designated specimen CMN 515 as the lectotype for Stegoceras validus in 1907.
facts.quote: Because the species was based on multiple specimens (a syntype series), CMN 515 was designated as the lectotype specimen by palaeontologist John Bell Hatcher in 1907.

facts.statement: Early researchers debated whether Stegoceras belonged to the ceratopsian or stegosaurian groups.
facts.quote: At this time, there was still uncertainty over which group of dinosaur Stegoceras belonged to, with both ceratopsians (horned dinosaurs) and stegosaurs (plated dinosaurs) as contenders.

facts.statement: The complete skull specimen UALVP 2 was discovered by George F. Sternberg in 1926 in the Belly River Group.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the Belly River Group by the American palaeontologist George F. Sternberg in 1926, and catalogued as specimen UALVP 2 in the University of Alberta Laboratory for Vertebrate Palaeontology.

facts.statement: Franz Nopcsa doubted the association of the skull and skeleton, suggesting they belonged to different animals.
facts.quote: Because the skull seemed so specialized compared to the rather "primitive"-looking skeleton, Nopcsa doubted whether these parts actually belonged together, and suggested the skull belonged to a nodosaur, the skeleton to an ornithopod, and the supposed gastralia (belly ribs) to a fish.

facts.statement: Stegoceras validum is known from the Dinosaur Park and Oldman Formations, while S. novomexicanum is known from the Fruitland and Kirtland Formations.
facts.quote: S. validum is known from the Dinosaur Park Formation and the Oldman Formation, whereas S. novomexicanum is known from the Fruitland and Kirtland Formation.

facts.statement: The species S. novomexicanum is debated and may not belong to the genus Stegoceras.
facts.quote: The remaining assigned species, S. novomexicanum, named in 2011 from fossils found in New Mexico, has also been debated, and may not belong to Stegoceras.

facts.statement: The specific name of S. browni honors Brown, who discovered the holotype specimen AMNH 5450 in Alberta.
facts.quote: The specific name honours Brown, who found the holotype specimen (specimen AMNH 5450 in the American Museum of Natural History) in Alberta.

facts.statement: In 1983, Galton and Hans-Dieter Sues transferred S. browni to the separate genus Ornatotholus.
facts.quote: In 1983, Galton and Hans-Dieter Sues moved S. browni to its own genus, Ornatotholus

facts.statement: In 2000, Robert M. Sullivan assigned S. edmontonensis and S. brevis to the genus Prenocephale.
facts.quote: In 2000, palaeontologist Robert M. Sullivan assigned S. edmontonensis and S. brevis to the genus Prenocephale

facts.statement: In 2003, Thomas E. Williamson and Thomas Carr considered Ornatotholus a dubious name or possibly a juvenile Stegoceras.
facts.quote: In 2003, Thomas E. Williamson and Thomas Carr considered Ornatotholus a nomen dubium, or perhaps a juvenile Stegoceras.

facts.statement: In 2021, Evans and colleagues transferred S. bexelli to the genus Sinocephale.
facts.quote: S. bexelli to Sinocephale in 2021 by Evans and colleagues.

facts.statement: In 2002, Williamson and Carr described a dome from the San Juan Basin, New Mexico (specimen NMMNH P-33983), considering it a juvenile pachycephalosaur of uncertain species.
facts.quote: In 2002, Williamson and Carr described a dome (specimen NMMNH P-33983 in the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science) from the San Juan Basin, New Mexico, which they considered a juvenile pachycephalosaur of uncertain species

facts.statement: In 2011, Steven E. Jasinski and Sullivan considered the New Mexico dome an adult and designated it the holotype of the new species Stegoceras novomexicanum.
facts.quote: In 2011, palaeontologist Steven E. Jasinski and Sullivan considered the specimen an adult, and made it the holotype of the new species Stegoceras novomexicanum

facts.statement: In 2016, Williamson and Stephen L. Brusatte restudied the S. novomexicanum holotype and found all involved specimens were juveniles, with paratypes belonging to a different taxon.
facts.quote: In 2016, palaeontologists Williamson and Stephen L. Brusatte restudied the holotype of S. novomexicanum and found that the paratypes did not belong to the same taxon as the holotype, and that all the involved specimens were juveniles.

facts.statement: In 2024, Steven L. Wick and Thomas M. Lehman described a juvenile Stegoceras specimen from the Aguja Formation of Texas based on morphometric analyses.
facts.quote: In 2024, a specimen of Stegoceras from the Aguja Formation of Texas was described, and assigned to Stegoceras based on morphometric analyses by palaeontologists Steven L. Wick and Thomas M. Lehman.

facts.statement: Stegoceras is estimated to have been about 2 to 2.5 meters long, comparable to the size of a goat.
facts.quote: Its length is estimated to have been about 2 to 2.5 m, comparable to the size of a goat.

facts.statement: The weight of Stegoceras has been estimated to be between 10 and 40 kilograms.
facts.quote: The weight has been estimated to be about 10 to 40 kg.

facts.statement: In 1974, Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska concluded that the gastralia of Stegoceras were ossified tendons based on similar structures found in Homalocephale.
facts.quote: In 1974, palaeontologists Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska concluded that the "gastralia" of Stegoceras were ossified tendons, after identifying such structures in the tail of the pachycephalosaur Homalocephale.

facts.statement: In 2016, Jasinski and Sullivan defended the validity of S. novomexicanum by presenting additional diagnostic features in the holotype despite agreeing some traits indicated a sub-adult stage.
facts.quote: In 2016, Jasinski and Sullivan defended the validity of S. novomexicanum; they agreed that some features used to diagnose the species were indicative of a sub-adult stage, but presented additional diagnostic features in the holotype that distinguish the species.

facts.statement: Dyer and colleagues suggested the S. novomexicanum holotype might be an immature Sphaerotholus goodwini because its unique traits disappeared during growth in S. validum.
facts.quote: Dyer and colleagues found that the S. novomexicanum holotype could be an immature Sphaerotholus goodwini, because the proposed unique traits of S. novomexicanum disappeared through ontogeny in S. validum.

facts.statement: The skull of Stegoceras was roughly triangular in side view with a relatively short snout.
facts.quote: The skull of Stegoceras was roughly triangular in shape when viewed from the side, with a relatively short snout.

facts.statement: The frontoparietal dome was broad with a relatively smooth surface, except for wrinkled sides.
facts.quote: The frontoparietal dome was broad and had a relatively smooth surface, with only the sides being rugose (wrinkled).

facts.statement: The large squamosal bone was not part of the dome, had a swollen back, and featured irregular tubercles and a row of nodes ending in small horns.
facts.quote: The squamosal was large, not part of the dome, and the back part was swollen. It was ornamented by irregularly spaced tubercles (or round outgrowths), and a row of nodes (knobs) extended along its upper edges, ending in a pointed tubercle (or small horn) on each side at the back of the skull.

facts.statement: Much of the skull, excluding the upper dome surface, was ornamented with nodes arranged in rows.
facts.quote: Except for the upper surface of the dome, much of the skull was ornamented with nodes, many arranged in rows.

facts.statement: The maxilla had foramina corresponding to tooth positions that served as passages for erupting replacement teeth.
facts.quote: The maxilla had a series of foramina that corresponded with each tooth position there, and these functioned as passages for erupting replacement teeth.

facts.statement: Stegoceras had heterodont (differentiated) and thecodont (socketed) teeth.
facts.quote: Stegoceras had teeth that were heterodont (differentiated) and thecodont (placed in sockets).

facts.statement: The front edges of the tooth crowns bore eight denticles, while the back edge bore nine to eleven.
facts.quote: The front edges of the crowns bore eight denticles (serrations), and the back edge bore nine to eleven.

facts.statement: Stegoceras skulls are distinguished by a pronounced parietosquamosal shelf, incipient doming that increases with age, inflated nasal bones, and specific tubercle and node ornamentation.
facts.quote: The skull of Stegoceras can be distinguished from those of other pachycephalosaurs by features such as its pronounced parietosquamosal shelf (though this became smaller with age), the "incipient" doming of its frontopariental (though the doming increased with age), its inflated nasal bones, its ornamentation of tubercles on the sides and back of the squamosal bones, rows of up to six tubercles on the upper side of each squamosal, and up to two nodes on the backwards projection of the parietal.

facts.statement: Stegoceras is distinct for its lack of nasal ornamentation and a reduced diastema.
facts.quote: It is also distinct in its lack of nasal ornamentation, and in having a reduced diastema.

facts.statement: S. novomexicanum differs from S. validum in having a more reduced and triangular parietal extension, larger supratemporal fenestrae, and roughly parallel suture contacts.
facts.quote: The skull of S. novomexicanum can be distinguished from that of S. validum in features such as the backwards extension of the parietal bone being more reduced and triangular, having larger supratemporal fenestrae (though this may be due to the possible juvenile status of the specimens), and having roughly parallel suture contacts between the squamosal and parietal.

facts.statement: Like other pachycephalosaurs, Stegoceras would have had a small beak.
facts.quote: Like other pachycephalosaurs, it would have had a small beak.

facts.statement: The articulation between successive dorsal vertebrae prevented sideways movement, making the vertebral column very rigid and strengthened by ossified tendons.
facts.quote: The articulation between the zygagophyses (articular processes) of successive dorsal (back) vertebrae appears to have prevented sideways movement of the vertebral column, which made it very rigid, and it was further strengthened by ossified tendons.

facts.statement: The scapula was longer than the humerus, with a slender, narrow, and slightly twisted blade following the rib contour.
facts.quote: The scapula (shoulder blade) was longer than the humerus (upper arm bone); its blade was slender and narrow, and slightly twisted, following the contour of the ribs.

facts.statement: The humerus had a slender shaft that was slightly twisted along its length and slightly bowed.
facts.quote: The humerus had a slender shaft, was slightly twisted along its length, and was slightly bowed.

facts.statement: Though incomplete, Stegoceras limbs were likely like other pachycephalosaurs, having five-fingered hands and four toes.
facts.quote: Though the limbs of Stegoceras are not completely known, they were most likely like other pachycephalosaurs in having five-fingered hands and four toes.

facts.statement: It is debated whether larger supratemporal fenestrae in S. novomexicanum are a species trait or due to juvenile status.
facts.quote: having larger supratemporal fenestrae (though this may be due to the possible juvenile status of the specimens)

facts.statement: In 1978, Dong Zhiming classified Stegoceras within the family Pachycephalosauridae, which included dome-headed pachycephalosaurs.
facts.quote: In 1978, the Chinese palaeontologist Dong Zhiming split Pachycephalosauria into two families; the dome-headed Pachycephalosauridae (including Stegoceras) and the flat-headed Homalocephalidae

facts.statement: In 1986, Paul Sereno grouped pachycephalosaurs like Stegoceras with ceratopsians into the suborder Marginocephalia based on cranial similarities.
facts.quote: In 1986, palaeontologist Paul Sereno supported the relationship between pachycephalosaurs and ceratopsians, and united them in the group Marginocephalia

facts.statement: A 2003 study by Sullivan suggested that Stegoceras was more primitive than fully-domed members of the subfamily Pachycephalosaurinae.
facts.quote: In 2003, Sullivan found Stegoceras itself to be more basal (or "primitive") than the "fully-domed" members of the subfamily Pachycephalosaurinae

facts.statement: A 2013 analysis by Evans et al. proposed that flat-headed pachycephalosaurs were more closely related to fully-domed taxa than to Stegoceras, suggesting flat heads might represent juveniles.
